title: Rescue collection — mixed reptiles: chronic regurgitation and weight loss
presentation: A rescue centre holding thirty reptiles of mixed species reports six animals — snakes and lizards — regurgitating and losing weight over three months, with two deaths. New arrivals are housed alongside residents.

stages.title: Assess the collection
stages.briefing: Affected animals: mid-body swelling in two snakes, regurgitation two to three days after feeding, progressive weight loss over three months, formed but scant faeces. Two deaths. Husbandry: temperatures and humidity appropriate on data-logger records, but shared feeding tongs and water bowls, no quarantine period, staff move between enclosures without changing gloves.
stages.prompt: Which findings point to an infectious problem rather than husbandry?

options.label: Several animals across different species affected in one collection
options.detail: A shared agent rather than a shared enclosure fault

options.label: Regurgitation two to three days after feeding with mid-body swelling
options.detail: Gastric disease in snakes

options.label: Shared tongs, bowls and no glove changes between enclosures
options.detail: A route for faecal-oral spread

options.label: Temperature and humidity within range on data loggers
options.detail: Important — it makes husbandry unlikely — but it is a negative

options.label: Scant formed faeces
options.detail: Expected in anything not retaining food

stages.explanation: Correct husbandry records are what make this interesting: the usual explanation for a wasting reptile is a cold, dry vivarium, and the loggers exclude it. Multiple species affected with shared equipment points to something transmissible, and post-feeding regurgitation with a palpable mid-body swelling localises it to the stomach.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: You can sample live animals and submit the two carcasses.

options.label: Faecal and gastric lavage cytology with acid-fast staining
options.detail: Cryptosporidium oocysts stain acid-fast

options.label: Cryptosporidium PCR on faeces and gastric washings
options.detail: Species-level confirmation, more sensitive than staining

options.label: Post-mortem with gastric histopathology
options.detail: Mucosal hyperplasia with organisms at the epithelial surface

options.label: Faecal flotation and direct smear for other parasites
options.detail: Mixed burdens are the norm in rescue collections

options.label: Screening of unaffected animals in the collection
options.detail: Defines how far it has spread

options.label: Inclusion body disease testing as the only investigation
options.detail: Worth doing in boids, but it does not explain lizards regurgitating too

options.label: Blood cultures on all thirty reptiles
options.detail: Disproportionate, and not how this diagnosis is made

stages.explanation: Acid-fast staining is cheap and fast, and the PCR is what confirms the species — Cryptosporidium serpentis in snakes and C. varanii in lizards behave differently and the distinction guides how hopeful you can be. Screening apparently healthy animals is not optional in a collection case: the animals with no signs decide whether this can be contained.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Acid-fast stains: numerous 5 µm oocysts in gastric lavage from three snakes and faeces from two lizards. PCR: Cryptosporidium serpentis in the snakes, C. varanii in the lizards. Post-mortem: marked gastric mucosal hyperplasia with organisms along the epithelial surface. Faecal flotation: pinworms in two lizards, no coccidia. Screening: four further animals with no clinical signs are PCR positive. Inclusion body disease testing negative in the two boids.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Cryptosporidiosis in the collection, with two species involved
options.detail: Organisms, PCR speciation and the gastric lesion

options.label: Subclinical shedders are present and maintaining transmission
options.detail: Four PCR-positive animals with no signs

options.label: Shared equipment and no quarantine allowed spread
options.detail: A faecal-oral organism in a collection with no barriers

options.label: Pinworms are incidental to this syndrome
options.detail: They do not cause gastric hyperplasia or regurgitation

options.label: Inclusion body disease explains the snakes
options.detail: Testing negative in both boids

options.label: Husbandry temperature deficits are the primary cause
options.detail: Data loggers show appropriate conditions

stages.explanation: The subclinical positives are the finding that changes the whole plan, because this parasite has no reliably curative treatment: control means identifying shedders, strict barrier husbandry and difficult decisions about long-term carriers. The negative IBD result is worth as much — it stops a second, unrelated investigation running in parallel.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Acid-fast oocysts with C. serpentis and C. varanii on PCR, gastric mucosal hyperplasia at post-mortem, four subclinical PCR-positive animals, appropriate husbandry records, IBD negative.

options.label: Collection-wide cryptosporidiosis with subclinical carriers
options.detail: Confirmed organism, its lesion and its reservoir

options.label: Inclusion body disease
options.detail: Negative on testing

options.label: Husbandry-related anorexia and regurgitation
options.detail: Excluded by the environmental records

options.label: Pinworm-associated enteropathy
options.detail: Incidental parasites that do not cause gastric disease

options.label: Gastric neoplasia
options.detail: Would not affect six animals of several species

stages.explanation: Naming it as a collection diagnosis is the point: cohorting positives, dedicated equipment per enclosure, disinfection that actually works against oocysts, a real quarantine period for arrivals, and an honest conversation about prognosis and euthanasia for wasting animals. Treating six reptiles individually would leave the centre reinfecting itself indefinitely.
